1.title: Designing Accessible Public Consultation Notices that Engage Communities
1.content: Consultation Notice project for Weston Consulting
1.subtitle: Weston Consulting
1.overview:
As part of Weston Consulting’s Community Consultation initiatives, this project focused on redesigning the Public Consultation Notice, a document distributed to residents within designated city areas to inform them about upcoming developments. The goal was to create a modern, approachable, and fully AODA-compliant design that communicates clearly to all residents, regardless of ability. 

By refining hierarchy, layout, and typographic structure, the new system balances accessibility with visual clarity, ensuring complex planning information feels transparent and easy to navigate. Printed on recyclable stock and mailed directly to households, the redesigned notice set a new benchmark for clarity, inclusivity, materiality, and civic communication, turning a procedural document into a meaningful tool for community engagement.
context: Strategic Objective: Redesigning the Public Consultation Notice to improve clarity and ensure 100% AODA compliance.
Target Audience: Residents within designated city areas, including those with visual or cognitive impairments.
Core Philosophy: Balancing technical planning requirements with visual transparency and inclusive design.
Primary Medium: Sustainable, 100% recyclable print mailers integrated with digital feedback portals.

2.title: Translating Architectural Lines into a Distinct Typographic Voice
2.subtitle: Espacio Ideal
2.overview:
The Espacio Ideal Typeface builds on the studio’s architectural language, translating spatial thinking into typographic form. My focus was on capturing the rhythm, proportion, and balance found in their architectural sketches, turning hand-drawn gestures into a structured, functional design system. Using Illustrator and FontForge, I developed a framework that merges expressive line work with architectural precision, resulting in a typeface that feels both crafted and intentional. 

Throughout development, I studied how contrast, geometry, and negative space could echo the studio’s design principles: measured, deliberate, and enduring. What began as a personal exploration evolved into a working typeface now used as the foundation of Espacio Ideal’s rebrand. It anchors their new logo and visual identity across print and environmental applications, carrying forward the same clarity, rhythm, and material honesty that define their architectural work.
context: Industry: Bespoke Architecture & Interior Design / Typographic Design.

The Challenge: A studio with architectural precision but a generic typographic voice. Their existing brand identity lacked a unique signature that could carry the emotional and technical weight of their 20-year legacy.

The Strategic Pivot: This project transformed hand-rendered architectural sketches into a proprietary all-caps display typeface. It moved from a conceptual exploration into the primary Visual DNA that now anchors the studio's logo, print materials, and global rebrand.

This wasn't just a design exercise; it was the creation of a Visual Signature. The resulting typeface now serves as the foundation for the studio’s entire rebrand, providing the connective tissue that ensures their legacy of craft is instantly recognizable across every digital and physical touchpoint.

4.title: Wild Lines of Stratford: A Wildlife-Inspired Beer Label Series
4.subtitle: Burlington Co.
4.overview:
Wild Lines of Stratford, a series of beer can labels created for a local brewery, translates local wildlife into a packaging system defined by geometric, angular illustration rendered in stark white-on-black contrast, infused with a personal illustrative style inspired by Alberto Giacometti. Three animals central to Stratford's environment: fox, swan, and racoons, are rendered through a single line, crystalline linework that echoes Giacometti's abstraction. 

Using Procreate to create these geometric drawings and Adobe Illustrator and InDesign for composition refinement, I created labels, and a small custom iconic that reinforces brand identity. The dark finish contrasting on the aluminum cans serve as a bold backdrop, allowing the white illustrations to command attention on shelf while communicating the intensity of the brewery's darker seasonal beer.
context: Industry: Craft Brewing & Premium Packaging.
The Challenge: Burlington Beers Co. required a visual identity for their darker, bolder seasonal release that could cut through a market saturated with loud, colourful labels.

The Market Gap: While the craft beer industry leans into high-saturation visual spectacle, a gap was identified for Restraint. By leading with geometric abstraction and monochromatic intensity, the packaging prioritizes the crystalline beauty of the season and the premium profile of the product.

accordionContextData.title: Deep Dive
accordionContextData.content: Wild Lines of Stratford translates local wildlife into a geometric packaging system inspired by the sculptural abstraction of Alberto Giacometti. By re-indexing the fox, swan, and raccoon through crystalline, single-line linework, I moved beyond traditional illustration to architect a brand identity rooted in structural tension and premium visual silence. The project’s maturity is defined by its transition from an academic process into a commercial asset. Originally a self-directed study, the system was acquired by Burlington Beers Co. to anchor their premium winter release. This journey from studio sketches to the shelves of Stratford, Ontario, proves that high-art intellectualism can be successfully engineered into a high-value, market-ready packaging system.

research: Stakeholder Alignment: Conducted feedback sessions with Burlington Beers Co. to align the geometric abstraction with their specific flavour positioning and label copy.
Market Intelligence: Analysed the Ontario craft beer landscape and the brewery’s existing roster to identify a gap for visual silence among high-saturation competitors.
Art-Historical Benchmarking: Indexed Alberto Giacometti’s sculptural work to translate organic forms into a crystalline visual shorthand, moving the brand toward a high-art aesthetic.

accordionResearchData.title: Deep Dive
accordionResearchData.content: The foundation of this project came from direct observation and artistic exploration. Walking through Stratford, I identified the most commonly seen animals: swans, foxes, and raccoons, that could serve as recognizable local symbols. My fascination with Alberto Giacometti's sculptural work at the time drove the visual direction, leading me to study his approach to form, proportion, and the energy of fragmented, angular lines. This research phase was validated through competitive benchmarking of the Ontario craft beer market and the brewery’s current portfolio. The primary insight was that minimalism serves as a premium signal. Through iterative meetings with the brewery, I ensured the aesthetic vision remained tethered to commercial requirements, transforming a personal study into a strategic market asset.

Ultimately demonstrating that workspace tools could serve as vehicles for personal expression. The project reinforced my belief that design can elevate everyday objects into meaningful experiences. 6.title: POSS Magazine: A Minimalist Editorial Exploration of Urban Culture
6.subtitle: YGTUT, Humble Magazine
6.overview:
POSS Magazine operates as a curated editorial object where typography, imagery, and cultural narrative converge into a disciplined visual system. Rooted in my experience growing up in Colombia, the magazine draws from the rhythms, tensions, and aesthetics of urban life, translating them into a minimal, gallery-like print language. The goal was not only to showcase imagery, but to build a refined editorial framework capable of elevating everyday cultural expression into a contemplative visual experience. 

The magazine functions as a series of controlled visual moments, balanced compositions, quiet grids, and measured contrasts, all working together to create an intentional narrative rhythm. Each spread serves as an independent visual object with its own tone and theme, yet all are unified through a shared aesthetic logic and layout. This systematic approach transformed the publication into more than a promotional artifact; POSS became a portable, minimal art piece that reflects both personal cultural perspective and contemporary urban movement.
context: Industry: Editorial Design, Magazine Branding, & Urban Culture.

The Challenge: Urban culture media often suffers from a maximalist default, a reliance on visual noise that fails to capture emotional depth and gritty authenticity of a the city this was based on: Cali, Colombia.

The Strategic Pivot: Leveraged the textures of my upbringing in Cali, Colombia, as a design source code. I joined forces with another designer to create a modular Editorial Protocol transforming the publication from a personal project into an internationally acquired asset for Humble Magazine (USA) and rapper, YG TUT’s (USA) social media campaign.

By treating the friction of my upbringing in Cali as a design source code, I transitioned from decorative layouts to a rigid grid system that created high-tension contrast against raw imagery. This project functioned as a technical stress test for editorial pacing, proving that visual silence could serve as a premium branding tool in a traditionally loud market. The resulting framework successfully moved from a personal exploration to a functional asset for Humble Magazine, reducing production lead times while maintaining brand cohesion. The system’s ultimate validation was its scalability; it was leveraged as the visual foundation for a social media campaign for American rapper YGTUT, proving that the same disciplined grid could house expressive, collage-driven digital content without losing structural integrity.

By proving that the grit of Cali could be indexed into a high-end design language, the solution provided a blueprint for how cultural authenticity can achieve professional credibility on a global stage.

11.overview:
The Catalogue Series translates Espacio Ideal’s architectural principles into a tactile editorial system. My focus centred on transforming spatial logic: proportion, rhythm, and material contrast, into a cohesive print language that felt intentional, and aligned with the studio’s ethos.

 Using Adobe InDesign, Illustrator & Photoshop, I developed a system defined by quiet and sharp typography, measured spacing, and a disciplined balance between sketches, photography, and material texture. Each catalogue functioned as an independent object with its own narrative purpose, yet all were unified through a shared logic that echoed Espacio Ideal’s architectural clarity. What began as a systematic exploration of form and sequence ultimately became the foundation for Espacio Ideal’s broader communication style. The Catalogue Series established the visual rhythm and editorial tone that later guided the studio’s digital transformation, providing a material-first blueprint for how their craft is communicated across mediums.
context: Industry: Bespoke Architecture & Interior Design.

The Challenge: A 20-year legacy trapped in a analogue image Existing catalogues were dense, convoluted, and visually outdated, filled with unrelated information and low-fidelity imagery that failed to reflect the studio’s modern precision.

The Strategic Pivot: This project served as the catalyst for the studio’s total rebrand. We moved from static, hard-to-navigate booklets to a modular Catalogue Series that established the visual and editorial DNA for the studio’s new international identity.

For decades, the studio’s primary communication tools were hindered by extreme information density and a lack of hierarchy; projects were buried under outdated imagery and analogue debt, making it difficult for clients to navigate the studio's true value. My role was to strip away this visual noise and architect a system that mirrored the studio’s physical approach: clean, intentional, and materially honest. Instead of a single, bloated document, I developed a modular editorial system where each project acts as a curated narrative. By implementing a disciplined grid and a Quiet Luxury typographic palette, I established a visual language that could finally translate their 20-year legacy and their future ambitions. This wasn't just a print redesign, it was the material-first blueprint for the studio’s entire rebrand. The logic we built here, the rhythm of the pages, the use of white space, and the focus on the architect’s hand, became the direct source code for the high-performance digital ecosystem that followed.

13.codeSnippet:
"""
Compare a Squarespace RSVP CSV with an internal invited list and export a color-coded report.

OUTPUT:
- comparison_report.xlsx
  - Sheet: "Guest List" (all invited, color-coded)
  - Sheet: "Summary" (counts)

COLOR KEY:
- Green  : Coming
- Yellow : No response
- Red    : Not coming

REQUIREMENTS:
- pandas
- openpyxl

EXPECTED INPUT COLUMNS (configurable below):
- Internal list CSV: email
- Squarespace RSVP CSV: email, rsvp_status
  where rsvp_status values include (case-insensitive):
  - "yes", "coming", "attending"
  - "no", "not coming", "declined"
"""
import pandas as pd
from openpyxl import load_workbook
from openpyxl.styles import PatternFill

# -------------------- CONFIG --------------------
INTERNAL_CSV = "internal_invited_list.csv"
RSVP_CSV = "squarespace_rsvp_list.csv"
INTERNAL_EMAIL_COL = "email"
RSVP_EMAIL_COL = "email"
RSVP_STATUS_COL = "rsvp_status"
OUTPUT_FILE = "comparison_report.xlsx"

COMING_VALUES = {"yes", "coming", "attending"}
NOT_COMING_VALUES = {"no", "not coming", "declined"}
# ------------------------------------------------

# Load CSVs with error handling
try:
    internal_df = pd.read_csv(INTERNAL_CSV)
    rsvp_df = pd.read_csv(RSVP_CSV)
except FileNotFoundError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
    exit(1)

# Validate required columns
if INTERNAL_EMAIL_COL not in internal_df.columns:
    print(f"Error: Column '{INTERNAL_EMAIL_COL}' not found in internal list")
    exit(1)
if RSVP_EMAIL_COL not in rsvp_df.columns or RSVP_STATUS_COL not in rsvp_df.columns:
    print(f"Error: Required columns not found in RSVP list")
    exit(1)

# Normalize emails
internal_df[INTERNAL_EMAIL_COL] = internal_df[INTERNAL_EMAIL_COL].str.strip().str.lower()
rsvp_df[RSVP_EMAIL_COL] = rsvp_df[RSVP_EMAIL_COL].str.strip().str.lower()

# Handle duplicates in RSVP data (keep most recent)
rsvp_df = rsvp_df.drop_duplicates(subset=[RSVP_EMAIL_COL], keep='last')

# Normalize RSVP status and handle NaN
rsvp_df[RSVP_STATUS_COL] = (
    rsvp_df[RSVP_STATUS_COL]
    .fillna("")
    .astype(str)
    .str.strip()
    .str.lower()
)

# Merge RSVP info onto internal list
merged = internal_df.merge(
    rsvp_df[[RSVP_EMAIL_COL, RSVP_STATUS_COL]],
    how="left",
    left_on=INTERNAL_EMAIL_COL,
    right_on=RSVP_EMAIL_COL,
)

# Determine final status
def resolve_status(status):
    if pd.isna(status) or status == "":
        return "No response"
    if status in COMING_VALUES:
        return "Coming"
    if status in NOT_COMING_VALUES:
        return "Not coming"
    return "No response"

merged["Final Status"] = merged[RSVP_STATUS_COL].apply(resolve_status)

# Summary counts
summary = merged["Final Status"].value_counts().reindex(
    ["Coming", "No response", "Not coming"], fill_value=0
).reset_index()
summary.columns = ["Status", "Count"]

# Write to Excel
with pd.ExcelWriter(OUTPUT_FILE, engine="openpyxl") as writer:
    merged.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Guest List", index=False)
    summary.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Summary", index=False)

# Apply colors
wb = load_workbook(OUTPUT_FILE)
ws = wb["Guest List"]

GREEN = PatternFill(start_color="C6EFCE", end_color="C6EFCE", fill_type="solid")
YELLOW = PatternFill(start_color="FFEB9C", end_color="FFEB9C", fill_type="solid")
RED = PatternFill(start_color="F4CCCC", end_color="F4CCCC", fill_type="solid")

status_col_idx = None
for i, cell in enumerate(ws[1], start=1):
    if cell.value == "Final Status":
        status_col_idx = i
        break

if status_col_idx:
    for row in ws.iter_rows(min_row=2):
        cell = row[status_col_idx - 1]
        if cell.value == "Coming":
            cell.fill = GREEN
        elif cell.value == "No response":
            cell.fill = YELLOW
        elif cell.value == "Not coming":
            cell.fill = RED

wb.save(OUTPUT_FILE)
print(f"Report generated: {OUTPUT_FILE}")
